chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
Selling an inherited property combines emotions and legal procedures. Between the settlement of the inheritance, decisions involving several heirs and tax aspects, it is better to move forward methodically and surround yourself well.

This guide outlines the main stages: the role of the liquidator, the checks before selling, the tax issues to be aware of, and the management of decisions between heirs.

Informative content, not legal or tax advice: hire a notary and, if necessary, an accountant. Each chapter ends with a lined “My Notes” page.

Selling an inherited property combines law, taxation, logistics and emotions. This guide clarifies who can sell and when, how to prepare and price the property, the tax issues, the decision to have multiple heirs and the delicate step of emptying the house.

Objective: conduct the sale calmly, within the rules, without conflict or emotion losing value.

chapters.title: The role of the liquidator and the prerequisites
chapters.objective: Know who can sell and when.
chapters.html:
Know who can sell and when.

In an estate, it is generally the liquidator (formerly “executor”) who administers the property and carries out the sale, according to the will and the law. Certain steps must precede the sale (settlement of the estate, publication of documents in the register).

  • Confirm who the liquidator is and their powers.
  • Check the property title and registration in the Land Register.
  • Understand what the will provides for the property.

In an estate, it is generally the liquidator who has the power to sell, once certain steps have been completed (acceptance of the charge, inventory, sometimes authorizations). Check who is authorized and what prerequisites are required BEFORE marketing, to avoid a questionable sale.

Emilie's advice

Before even thinking about the price, have the notary confirm who has the authority to sell and what steps must be taken. Selling too early or without the right powers creates costly bottlenecks.

chapters.title: Prepare the property and set the price
chapters.objective: Sell ​​a property that is often old or unoccupied.
chapters.html:
Sell a property that is often old or unoccupied.

An inherited property is sometimes aging, furnished or unoccupied for a while. Prepare it like any sale: empty, clean, repair the essentials, then set a price based on a comparative analysis.

  • Have the current market value (ACM) assessed.
  • Decide what to gut, repair or sell as is.
  • Consider an inspection to know the true condition and avoid disputes.

An inherited property is often old, furnished or unoccupied: cleaning, decluttering and some targeted repairs can significantly improve the price. Price based on comparative analysis, not sentimental value or municipal assessment.

Emilie's advice

Don't sell off an inherited property out of haste, but don't overinvest in renovations either. Light preparation and fair pricing often yield the best bottom line for heirs.

chapters.title: Tax issues to know
chapters.objective: Anticipate the tax linked to inheritance and sales.
chapters.html:
Anticipate the tax linked to inheritance and sales.

The taxation of an inherited property can be complex: depending on the case, a capital gain can be calculated from the value at death, the main residence can benefit from an exemption, etc. The rules depend on the specific situation.

Don't assume anything: an accountant or tax specialist, with the notary, will tell you what applies and how to legally minimize the tax.

The taxation of an inheritance can be complex: capital gains, value at death, deadlines. A mistake can be costly. Consult a notary and an accountant to find out the implications before selling - it's an investment that avoids unpleasant tax surprises.

Emilie's advice

Talk to an accountant BEFORE you sell, not after. The tax decisions of an inheritance need to be planned: once the sale is made, certain options are no longer available.

chapters.title: Deciding on multiple heirs
chapters.html:
Manage collective decisions without conflict.

When several heirs are involved, the decisions (to sell or not, at what price, which offers to accept) must be made together. Disagreements are frequent and emotionally charged.

  • Clarify early on who decides what (often the liquidator, in consultation).
  • Rely on facts (ACM, notary's opinion) to depersonalize decisions.
  • Communicate regularly to avoid misunderstandings.

When several heirs are involved, decisions (to sell or not, price, calendar) must be taken together. Clarify decision-making and sharing early on; a neutral intermediary (notary, broker) helps to stay on track without emotion blocking the sale.

Emilie's advice

Base decisions on neutral facts (price analysis, notary's opinion) rather than on emotions. A professional third party often helps heirs reach a peaceful understanding.

chapters.title: Emptying the house: practical and emotional aspects
chapters.html:
Manage content before sale.

Before selling an inherited property, it is often necessary to empty - a stage loaded with emotions as much as logistics.

  • Sort : keep, give, sell, throw away.
  • Provide time and, if possible, divide the task among heirs.
  • Document the objects of value (succession).
  • Consider a estate sale or specialized services.

A decluttered and clean house presents better and sells more easily.

Emptying the house is a step loaded with emotion as well as logistics: sort (keep, donate, sell, throw away), document valuable objects and, if necessary, get help. Don't rush sorting, but don't let the sale drag on for months either.

Emilie's advice

Don't rush the sorting out of emotion, but don't let it delay the sale for months either. Set a realistic deadline and, if necessary, get help.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Confirm the liquidator and the powers of sale with the notary.
  2. Have the market value assessed (ACM).

Within 30 days

  1. Consult an accountant on tax impacts.
  2. Prepare the property and structure decisions between heirs.

Then

  1. Put on sale with support adapted to the estate.

First steps

  1. Confirm who the liquidator is and what prerequisites are required.
  2. Consult notary/accountant on taxation before selling.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Liquidator: person who administers the estate and carries out the sale.
  • Land register: public register of real estate rights.
  • ACM: comparative market analysis to set the current value.
  • Capital gain: possible tax depending on the value at death and the use of the property.
  • Principal residence exemption: tax relief possible depending on the situation.
  • Liquidator: person authorized to administer and sell the assets of the estate.
  • Capital gain: taxable profit realized on the sale, according to the value at death.
  • Joint inheritance: property held jointly by the heirs.
  • Comparative analysis: objective basis for setting the price.
  • Estate sale: liquidation of contents before marketing.
